questions.stem: The archaeologist V. Gordon Childe described the change from village farming to the first cities as the:
options: broad spectrum revolution
secondary products revolution
hilly flanks revolution
urban revolution
questions.explanation: Childe called the rise of cities the urban revolution and listed features such as surplus, specialisation, monumental buildings and writing. The broad spectrum revolution is Kent Flannery's idea about foraging before farming, not the rise of cities.

questions.stem: Which feature would most historians use to distinguish an early civilisation from a large farming village?
options: A diet that depends on plants and animals that have been domesticated
Permanent houses built in one place and occupied all year round
The use of polished stone tools, grinding stones and fired clay pots for cooking
Full-time specialists such as scribes and priests, fed from a food surplus
questions.explanation: Farming villages already had domesticated food, permanent houses and pottery. What marks a civilisation is a surplus large enough to support people who do not farm, such as scribes, priests and craft workers, along with institutions to manage them.

questions.stem: A historian argues that calling Mesopotamia the ‘cradle of civilisation’ is misleading. Which evidence best supports that view?
options: Uruk grew to become one of the largest settlements of the fourth millennium BCE
Mesopotamian farmers relied on irrigation canals fed by the Tigris and Euphrates
Complex societies also arose separately in places such as China and the Americas
Sumerian scribes wrote many of their texts in a script based on wedge shapes
questions.explanation: The ‘cradle’ label implies civilisation spread outward from one source. Independent developments in China, Mesoamerica and the Andes show complex societies arose in several places. The size of Uruk supports Mesopotamia's importance rather than challenging the label.

questions.stem: The name ‘Mesopotamia’ comes from Greek and means:
options: the land of the black soil
the land beyond the great sea
the land between the rivers
the land of the two crowns
questions.explanation: Mesopotamia means ‘between the rivers’, referring to the Tigris and Euphrates. ‘Black soil’ describes how Egyptians called their own land Kemet, after the dark silt of the Nile.

questions.stem: Farmers in southern Mesopotamia had to build canals and irrigation channels mainly because:
options: rainfall was too low for crops and the rivers flooded at the wrong time of year
the rivers flooded gently every autumn just before the seed was sown each year
heavy winter rains regularly washed the topsoil of the plain into the Persian Gulf
the land was hilly, so water had to be carried up to fields on the slopes
questions.explanation: The south received too little rain for farming, and the Tigris and Euphrates flooded in spring, close to harvest, often violently. Canals stored and spread water when crops needed it. The gentle, well-timed flood describes the Nile, not the Mesopotamian rivers.

questions.stem: Southern Mesopotamia had fertile soil and plenty of clay and reeds, but it lacked:
options: date palms, fish and marsh birds as sources of food
stone, timber and metal ores, which had to be traded for
a flat floodplain that was suitable for growing grain
rivers deep enough to be used to move heavy goods by boat
questions.explanation: The alluvial plain had no good building stone, little timber and no metal ores, so these came through long-distance trade. The flat plain, navigable rivers and marsh foods were advantages the region did have.

questions.stem: A text from a Sumerian city records falling wheat yields and a shift to growing barley over several centuries. The most likely environmental cause is:
options: the Euphrates freezing over for longer each winter
a volcanic eruption that buried the plain under ash
salt building up in the soil after long use of irrigation
a sudden rise in yearly rainfall that waterlogged the fields
questions.explanation: Irrigation water in a hot climate evaporates and leaves salts behind. Barley tolerates salt better than wheat, so a shift towards barley is the classic sign of salinisation. Southern Mesopotamia had little rain and its rivers did not freeze.

questions.stem: A cylinder seal from Mesopotamia was used by:
options: burning it as an offering to the patron god of the city's temple
rolling it over wet clay to leave a design that marked ownership
pressing its sharp end into clay to form wedge-shaped signs
stamping coins with the face of the ruler of the city-state
questions.explanation: Cylinder seals were carved stone cylinders rolled across clay to leave a continuous impression, marking ownership or sealing goods and documents. Cuneiform signs were made with a reed stylus, and coins did not yet exist.

questions.stem: The Standard of Ur shows scenes of war on one side and peace on the other. As evidence, it is most useful for showing:
options: how the elite wished to present the king, his army and his wealth
the exact number of soldiers who served in the army of Ur
the daily diet and housing of the ordinary farmers of Sumer's cities
the words the king of Ur spoke to his army before battle
questions.explanation: The Standard is elite art, so it shows how rulers wanted power and prosperity to be seen: chariots, captives, tribute and banqueting. It contains no counts, speeches or details of ordinary homes, so it cannot support those claims.

questions.stem: The Warka Vase from Uruk shows rows of plants, animals and naked men carrying offerings up to a goddess. Historians mostly use it as evidence of:
options: the military conquest of Uruk by the kings of Akkad
the system of laws that governed trade between cities
the methods used to build the ziggurat of Ur-Nammu
the link between farming surplus and the temple in Uruk
questions.explanation: The vase moves from crops and herds up to offerings presented to Inanna, showing produce flowing to the temple. It predates the Akkadian conquest and says nothing about laws or the later ziggurat of Ur.

questions.stem: A ziggurat was:
options: a royal palace with a walled garden courtyard
a burial chamber cut into the side of a cliff
a market hall where merchants traded grain
a stepped temple platform built of mud brick
questions.explanation: Ziggurats were massive stepped platforms of mud brick, with a shrine on top, dedicated to a city's god. The ziggurat of Ur, built under Ur-Nammu, is the best-preserved example.

questions.stem: Which dating method gives an absolute date for an object?
options: Seriation of pottery styles
Typology of bronze weapons
Radiocarbon dating of charcoal
Stratigraphy of the soil layers
questions.explanation: Radiocarbon dating measures the decay of carbon-14 in once-living material and gives a date in years, with a margin of error. Stratigraphy, seriation and typology only place things in order, which is relative dating.

questions.stem: An archaeologist finds a clay tablet in a layer below a layer that holds Akkadian pottery. Using stratigraphy, she can conclude that the tablet:
options: was most likely deposited before the Akkadian pottery
was made at exactly the same time as the Akkadian pottery
was certainly written in the Akkadian language
can be given a precise calendar date in years BCE
questions.explanation: The law of superposition says lower layers were usually laid down first, so the tablet is probably older. Stratigraphy is relative dating: it gives an order, not a calendar date, and says nothing about the tablet's language.

questions.stem: Radiocarbon dating could be used to date which of these finds from the Royal Cemetery at Ur?
options: Wood from a wagon placed in a tomb
A gold helmet beaten from sheet metal
A lapis lazuli bead from Afghanistan
A clay tablet baked hard in a fire
questions.explanation: Radiocarbon dating works only on material that was once alive, such as wood, bone, seeds or textiles. Gold and lapis lazuli are minerals, and fired clay is dated by other methods such as thermoluminescence.

questions.stem: Who led the excavation of the Royal Cemetery at Ur in the 1920s and early 1930s?
options: Leonard Woolley
Howard Carter
Austen Henry Layard
André Parrot
questions.explanation: Leonard Woolley excavated Ur for the British Museum and the University of Pennsylvania and uncovered the royal tombs and death pits. Layard dug at Nimrud and Nineveh, and Parrot at Mari.

questions.stem: In the ‘death pits’ at Ur, Woolley found dozens of attendants buried with royal figures such as Puabi. Which inference from this evidence is best supported?
options: Every adult in Ur expected to be buried in a richly furnished tomb
The attendants were prisoners of war captured in battle with Akkad
The burials prove that the Sumerians believed in reincarnation after death
Some rulers had the authority to have others die and be buried with them
questions.explanation: Many attendants buried in the pits with jewellery, instruments and wagons show the extreme power of some elite individuals over others. Most people of Ur had simple graves, the tombs predate Akkad, and nothing in them shows a belief in reincarnation.

questions.stem: Robert Braidwood's ‘hilly flanks’ theory argues that farming began:
options: in the hills around the Fertile Crescent, where wild wheat and goats lived
in desert oases, where people and animals crowded together in a drought
on the southern floodplain, where irrigation made grain growing possible
in coastal areas, where rising seas forced fishers to grow their own food
questions.explanation: Braidwood, who excavated Jarmo in the Zagros foothills, argued that farming arose where the wild ancestors of crops and animals lived naturally. The oasis theory, with drought crowding people and animals together, belongs to Childe.

questions.stem: V. Gordon Childe's ‘oasis theory’ suggests that agriculture began because:
options: hunters began to rely on a wider range of smaller foods such as fish
a drier climate brought people, plants and animals together near water
people living in the hills began to tend the wild grains they gathered
a growing population on the coast pushed groups into marginal lands
questions.explanation: Childe argued that as the climate dried, people and animals gathered at oases, and close contact led to domestication. Tending wild grains in the hills is Braidwood's view; pressure on marginal lands is Lewis Binford's.

questions.stem: Lewis Binford's theory differs from Braidwood's because Binford argued that farming began:
options: as people and animals were forced together around shrinking water sources
after Sumerian priests developed irrigation to grow grain for the temples
when population pressure pushed people out of rich areas into marginal ones
where wild cereals and animals already lived in the hills of the region
questions.explanation: Binford saw farming as a response to stress: as groups in rich areas grew, some were pushed into marginal zones where they had to cultivate food. Braidwood stressed the natural habitat of wild cereals rather than pressure, and Childe stressed drought and oases.

questions.stem: Which group of plants and animals was among the first to be domesticated in the Fertile Crescent?
options: Wheat, barley, sheep and goats
Rice, millet, pigs and silkworms
Maize, beans, llamas and turkeys
Potatoes, cotton, horses and camels
questions.explanation: Emmer and einkorn wheat, barley, sheep and goats were domesticated early in south-west Asia. Rice and millet were domesticated in China, and maize and llamas in the Americas.

questions.stem: Why did the growth of a food surplus in Mesopotamia lead to social stratification?
options: Grain could not be stored for long, so no group could build up any wealth
Those who controlled the stored surplus gained power over those who produced it
Every family grew exactly the same amount, so all the wealth was shared out equally
A surplus allowed people to stop farming and return to hunting and gathering
questions.explanation: Surplus grain could be stored, taxed and redistributed, and the temples and elites who controlled it gained wealth and authority. Unequal control of resources is what produced a hierarchy of classes.

questions.stem: In Sumerian cities, potters, metal workers and weavers could work at their crafts full time because:
options: the cities banned anyone from growing their own food
temples and palaces fed them from stored rations of grain
they were paid in silver coins minted by the city's king
each worker kept a large farm worked by their own children
questions.explanation: Temple and palace households issued rations of barley, oil and wool to dependent workers, which freed them from farming. Coins did not exist yet; silver was weighed as a measure of value.

questions.stem: A tablet from Uruk lists rations of barley given to 50 weavers, 12 potters and 4 brewers working for the temple. What does the tablet best show about early urban society?
options: Most of the city's people worked as weavers, potters and brewers
Workers were free to sell their goods at a market in the city
The temple had no role in the economy outside religious rituals
A central institution managed specialised labour using its surplus
questions.explanation: The list shows the temple organising and feeding specialist workers from its stores, a key feature of the urban revolution. One list cannot show the makeup of the whole population, and it records rations, not market sales.

questions.stem: The earliest writing in Mesopotamia, found at Uruk from about 3200 BCE, was used mainly to:
options: record goods, rations and accounts
write down hymns and long love poems
tell the story of Gilgamesh
record the laws of the kings
questions.explanation: The first tablets from Uruk are almost all administrative: lists of grain, animals, workers and rations. Literature and law codes were written down centuries later, once the script could record full sentences of language.

questions.stem: Cuneiform writing was made by:
options: carving signs into wood with a bronze knife
scratching marks onto bones heated in fire
pressing a cut reed stylus into soft clay
painting ink onto papyrus with a brush
questions.explanation: Cuneiform means ‘wedge-shaped’: a scribe pressed a reed stylus into damp clay. Ink on papyrus was Egyptian, and writing on heated bones is the Shang oracle bone practice in China.

questions.stem: Over time, cuneiform changed from pictures of objects to wedge signs that could stand for sounds. The most important result was that scribes could:
options: write on papyrus and parchment instead of on clay tablets
record only numbers, since words had become too hard to show
write whole sentences, names and other languages such as Akkadian
stop training in schools because anyone could read the new signs
questions.explanation: Signs that stood for syllables let scribes record grammar, personal names and different languages, so the script was adapted for Akkadian. Cuneiform still needed years of training and stayed mostly on clay.

questions.stem: A student claims that written sources from Sumer give a balanced picture of society. Which response is best?
options: Tablets cannot be dated in any way, so they are of no use to historians at all
Scribes recorded only myths, so the tablets tell us nothing about the economy
Most texts were written by scribes for temples and rulers, so they reflect elite concerns
Writing was taught in every village, so tablets record the views of all the social groups
questions.explanation: Literacy was limited to trained scribes working for temples, palaces and wealthy households, so texts mostly show elite and administrative interests. Tablets are very useful and include many economic records; they are just not a voice for everyone.

questions.stem: Scribes in Mesopotamia were trained in schools known in Sumerian as the edubba, which means:
options: ‘great house’
‘house of the king’
‘tablet house’
‘house of the god’
questions.explanation: The edubba, or ‘tablet house’, was where boys copied signs and texts to learn cuneiform. The temple was the god's house and the palace (é-gal) was the ‘great house’.

questions.stem: In early Sumer, each city-state was believed to belong to:
options: the king of the largest city
the families who farmed it
the assembly of its elders
its patron god or goddess
questions.explanation: Sumerians believed each city was the property of a god, such as Nanna at Ur or Inanna at Uruk, and the ruler governed on the god's behalf. This is why temples were central to the economy.

questions.stem: The Sumerian title ‘lugal’, used for the ruler of a city-state, literally means:
options: ‘god on earth’
‘big man’
‘chief priest’
‘shepherd’
questions.explanation: Lugal combines ‘lu’ (man) and ‘gal’ (big). Other titles were en, often linked to a priestly role, and ensi, a governor ruling for the god. Kings were described as shepherds, but that is not what lugal means.

questions.stem: Some historians argue that early Sumerian rulers were ‘priest-kings’. This means rulers:
options: were worshipped as gods during their lives by the people of every city
combined religious duties for the city's god with political leadership
were chosen by lot each year from among the priests of every temple
ruled only over religious matters, while elders made political decisions
questions.explanation: The idea is that early rulers led temple ritual as well as governing, so religious and political power were joined. Kings claiming to be living gods came later, with Naram-Sin of Akkad and Shulgi of Ur.

questions.stem: Thorkild Jacobsen argued that early Sumer had a form of ‘primitive democracy’. Which evidence did he use?
options: Tax lists showing that every citizen paid the same amount to the temple
Law codes stating that kings were elected by all free men every year
Royal inscriptions in which kings refuse to fight without a public vote
Literary texts in which a ruler consults the elders and the men of the city
questions.explanation: Jacobsen pointed to myths and epics in which rulers and gods take matters to assemblies, such as Gilgamesh putting a question of war to the elders and the young men of Uruk. No tax lists, law codes or inscriptions record elected kings.

questions.stem: In The Epic of Gilgamesh, Gilgamesh is king of which city?
options: Uruk
Ur
Babylon
Nineveh
questions.explanation: Gilgamesh is the king of Uruk, and the epic ends with praise of the city's great walls. The fullest surviving version was found on tablets at Nineveh, which is why students sometimes mix the two up.

questions.stem: At the end of The Epic of Gilgamesh, the hero has failed to win eternal life. The epic suggests he can still be remembered through:
options: the great walls and city of Uruk that he built
the plant of youth that he brings home safely
the sons who rule after him in the city of Kish
the gold statue the gods set up in his honour
questions.explanation: Gilgamesh loses the plant of rejuvenation to a snake, then returns and shows the walls of Uruk, implying that lasting fame comes from human achievement. This reflects the value placed on the city and its king.

questions.stem: Gilgamesh is described as two-thirds god and one-third human, and he oppresses the people of Uruk until the gods create Enkidu. What does this suggest about Sumerian views of kingship?
options: The people of Uruk had the legal right to remove a cruel king
Kings had no link to the gods and ruled only by military force
Kings had great power, but the gods were expected to limit their abuses
Kings were ordinary citizens elected by the people of Uruk for a fixed term
questions.explanation: The story presents the king as semi-divine and powerful, yet the gods respond to the people's complaints by creating Enkidu to restrain him. Nothing in the epic describes elections or a legal right to depose a king.

questions.stem: The flood story in The Epic of Gilgamesh is told to Gilgamesh by:
options: Enkidu
Humbaba
Shamhat
Utnapishtim
questions.explanation: Utnapishtim survived the flood by building a boat and was granted eternal life by the gods; he tells Gilgamesh the story. Humbaba is the guardian of the Cedar Forest whom Gilgamesh and Enkidu kill.

questions.stem: Sargon of Akkad, who came to power about 2334 BCE, is best known for:
options: creating the first empire uniting Sumer and Akkad
writing the first law code of Mesopotamia
building the great Royal Library in the city of Nineveh
inventing the cuneiform writing system
questions.explanation: Sargon conquered the Sumerian city-states and lands beyond, forming what is usually called the first empire. The first surviving law code is Ur-Nammu's, and the library at Nineveh belonged to Ashurbanipal, about 1,700 years later.

questions.stem: According to the later Legend of Sargon, before he became king Sargon served as:
options: general in the army of Uruk
cupbearer to Ur-Zababa, king of Kish
high priest of the moon god at Ur
governor of the city of Lagash
questions.explanation: The legend tells that Sargon was set adrift in a reed basket as a baby, raised by a water-drawer and became cupbearer to King Ur-Zababa of Kish before seizing power. These are later stories, so historians treat them with caution.

questions.stem: Sargon appointed his daughter Enheduanna as high priestess of the moon god Nanna at Ur. Historians see this as significant mainly because it:
options: tied a key Sumerian religious centre to the Akkadian royal family
showed that women could not hold any religious office before Sargon
moved the capital of the Akkadian Empire from Akkad to Ur
ended the worship of Sumerian gods across the conquered cities
questions.explanation: Placing a royal daughter in a leading Sumerian priesthood joined Akkadian rule to Sumerian religion and helped legitimise the conquest. Enheduanna is also remembered for hymns attributed to her. Sumerian gods continued to be worshipped.

questions.stem: Which change did Sargon introduce to help him control his conquests?
options: A council of elected Sumerian governors in each city
A single coin currency used throughout the empire
A ban on writing in any language except Sumerian
Akkadian officials and a standing army loyal to the king
questions.explanation: Sargon installed loyal Akkadians in conquered cities and maintained a large standing army; his inscriptions boast of thousands of men eating daily before him. Coinage did not exist yet, and Akkadian, not Sumerian, became important in administration.

questions.stem: The Epic of the King of Battle describes Sargon marching to Anatolia to protect merchants. A historian should treat this text cautiously mainly because it:
options: was written by a merchant who was an eyewitness to the march
survives only in Greek translation made many centuries later
contradicts every surviving inscription of Sargon's reign
is a later literary work that celebrates Sargon as a heroic model
questions.explanation: The epic survives in later copies and was written to glorify Sargon as an ideal warrior king, so it reflects how later Mesopotamians remembered him. It is not an eyewitness account and it survives in cuneiform, not Greek.

questions.stem: The Chronicle of Early Kings praises Sargon's conquests but also states that in his old age all the lands revolted against him. What does this show about how later sources represented Sargon?
options: They ignored his conquests and recorded only his religious works
They could show him as a great conqueror and as a ruler punished for faults
They agreed that Sargon's reign was peaceful and stable from beginning to end
They were written by Sargon himself to defend his record as king
questions.explanation: The Babylonian chronicle mixes praise of Sargon's power with a moral lesson: it links the revolt to his offence against Babylon's god. Later writers used Sargon's story for their own purposes, so his representation is not simply heroic.

questions.stem: Ur-Nammu, founder of the Third Dynasty of Ur about 2112 BCE, is known for:
options: building the walls of Uruk for Gilgamesh
moving the capital of Sumer to Babylon
a law code and the great ziggurat of Ur
conquering Egypt and the Nile Delta
questions.explanation: The oldest surviving law code is credited to Ur-Nammu (some scholars assign it to his son Shulgi), and he began the ziggurat of Ur. His laws often set fines in silver rather than physical punishments. Babylon became important only under the later Amorite kings.

questions.stem: Under Shulgi, Ur III kept tens of thousands of tablets recording animals arriving at and leaving the centre at Puzrish-Dagan. These records best show that the Ur III state:
options: had no taxes and relied only on gifts from foreign rulers
was a loose group of cities with no shared administration
left the management of herds to nomadic Amorite tribes
ran a highly centralised economy through a large bureaucracy
questions.explanation: Puzrish-Dagan collected and redistributed livestock from across the state, tracked by scribes in great detail. This is evidence of strong central control, standard weights and measures, and a large bureaucracy. Shulgi was also worshipped as a god.

questions.stem: The Third Dynasty of Ur came to an end about 2004 BCE when:
options: the Hittites sacked the city after a long march down the Euphrates
the Assyrians under Tiglath-pileser III made Ur into a province
Sargon of Akkad defeated Lugalzagesi and seized the cities of Sumer
the Elamites captured Ur and took its last king, Ibbi-Sin, prisoner
questions.explanation: Weakened by Amorite pressure and the breakaway of provinces, Ur fell to the Elamites, who carried off Ibbi-Sin. The Hittite sack was of Babylon in 1595 BCE, and Sargon's conquest came before Ur III.
